item.description: In the Research Article e9668428, Qiaobao Zhang, Xueliang Sun, Changhong Wang, and co-workers describe the unique three-stage delithiation pathway of Li5FeO4 in an all-solid-state reaction environment: low-potential lattice oxygen oxidation, coupled oxygen/iron oxidation, and lattice oxygen oxidation accompanied by iron reduction. Nanosized Li5FeO4 compensates for irreversible lithium loss in silicon anodes, enabling high-energy-density ASSBs.

item.title: Atroposelective Access to Bicyclic Peptides via an Amide Photocaging Strategy
item.description:
Ansamers are an atypical class of atropisomers (Pansa /Mansa ) and stereoselective synthesis of its two conformational isomers is challenging. We introduce a photocaged amide protection strategy: photolabile groups in monocycles reversibly modulate amide geometry, biasing macrolactamization to selectively give Pansa or Mansa . Computational studies show Mansa proceeds via a lower-energy transition state. The method works across diverse sequences and tolerates key functional groups, confirming its robustness and broad utility.


ABSTRACT

The fungal toxin α-amanitin is a structurally complex bicyclic octapeptide featuring a macrolactam scaffold stabilized by a tryptathionine crossbridge critical for its conformational stability. Building on the prior development of the ansamer (Pansa/Mansa ) nomenclature for an amatoxin isomer classification, the challenge of atroposelective synthesis of both isomers, the natural Pansa and non-natural Mansa, remained. This work introduces an innovative amide bond photocaging strategy implemented on monocyclic peptide precursors, enabling the control of conformational selectivity during bicyclization to achieve the directed formation of the Pansa or Mansa atropisomer. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics simulations provide strong theoretical support for the experimentally observed atroposelectivity in Mansa formation. The methodology described could establish a paradigm for conformational control in the synthesis of bicyclic peptides, with implications for a rational conformational design across diverse peptide architectures.

item.title: Inside Front Cover: Operando Identification of Ni dz2 Orbital Descriptor Governing Urea Oxidation Electrocatalysis
item.description: Interfacial π-π coupling between nickel phthalocyanine (NiPc) and curved carbon nanotubes enables dynamic regulation of the Ni 3d electronic structure during urea oxidation. Rather than conventional oxidation-state evolution, electrochemical activation redistributes the Ni 3d orbitals while preserving the active Ni(II) site. The Ni 3dz2 occupancy serves as a quantitative descriptor of intrinsic activity, revealing catalyst-support mediated frontier orbital engineering as a strategy for rational electrocatalyst design. More in the Research Article e4712106, Heng-Liang Wu, Hui-Lung Chen, Hao Ming Chen, and co-workers.

item.title: Outside Back Cover: Hydroxyl‐Bridged Phosphorus Doping‐Induced Charge Polarization Enhancing Electron Delocalization for Efficient Photoreduction of CO2
item.description: OH-bridged P atom doped carbon nitride features a unique 2N–P=OOH microstructure in heptazine units. P doping disrupts π-π conjugation of carbon nitride. OH-modified P doping further leads to spatial charge polarization enhancing the delocalization of electrons. Water interacts with P-OH to enable chemical adsorption of CO2. This collectively supports the efficient CO2 photoreduction to CO. More in Research Article e3254251, Hainan Shi, Haozhi Wang, Xinwen Guo, and co-workers.

item.title: Inside Front Cover: Transformation of Active Sites on Cobalt Sulfide Nanoclusters With Similar Nuclearities
item.description: In Communication e5734835, Nan Yan, Bin Chen, Zhikun Wu, and co-workers present a dual-ligand strategy to tune the dimensions and ligand distributions of atomically precise cobalt sulfide nanoclusters. Ligand habitat segregation and active-site interconversion among cobalt, thiolate sulfur, and bare sulfur are revealed. Furthermore, the dipole-moment direction and coordination number are identified as intrinsic spatial descriptors, offering new insights into cobalt sulfide catalysis.

item.title: The Crystal Structural Foundation of the “Rippled” Beta‐Sheet
item.description:
The rippled beta-sheet was postulated by Pauling and Corey in 1953. Unlike with the closely related pleated beta-sheet, it took decades for the conclusive experimental evidence for the motif to emerge. Over the past 5 years, our crystallographic work established the rippled antiparallel beta-sheet as a structural motif with general features, capable of accommodating the majority of the canonical amino acids.


ABSTRACT

The “rippled” β-sheet was theorized by Pauling and Corey in 1953, yet, unlike the pleated β-sheet, remained obscure for well over half a century. From 2011 onward, the studies conducted independently by the Schneider, Nilsson and Raskatov laboratories provided the critical nucleus of biophysical data to support the viability of the rippled sheet, stimulating the ensuing x-ray structural work. The first rippled sheet crystal structure was reported by us in 2022, 69 years after its prediction. The field has since witnessed a rapid expansion in terms of both crystal structural understanding and conceptual innovation concerning novel motif types. We have reported fifteen rippled sheet crystal structures thus far. Of the 20 canonical amino acids, our published studies have established 13 to be ripple-genic, that is, capable of forming rippled sheets. Reported ripple-genic systems range from tri- to heptapeptide in length. Among the newest advances are the mixed chirality motifs, capable of forming rippled sheets from single components, as well as conformationally locked rippled sheet macrocycles. The maturing crystal structural foundation is expected to stimulate many new and interesting applications including biomaterials, as well as molecular recognition of intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides.

item.title: Inside Back Cover: Hybrid‐Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry Probes Atomic‐Scale Insight Into Selective C─C Bond Cleavage in PET Upcycling
item.description: In the Research Article e1863949, Jyh-Chiang Jiang, Jong Sung Jin, Myong Yong Choi, and co-workers developed CO2 laser-engineered Ru single-atoms on NiO regulate reaction intermediates and direct selective formate production from ethylene glycol, a key polyethylene terephthalate (PET)-derived monomer. Advanced hybrid-SIMS and operando spectroscopy provide molecular-level insights into PET upcycling, offering new principles for catalyst design and sustainable circular-carbon technologies.

item.title: Inside Back Cover: Transient Potential‐Driven Ir‐Site Response Regulates Lattice‐Oxygen Participation
item.description: The potential-driven dynamic response of Ir sites during acidic oxygen evolution is revealed. In the Research Article e8928500, Wei Zhang, Linlin Cao, Tao Yao, and co-workers use operando energy-dispersive X-ray absorption spectroscopy to track transient electronic and local structural evolution, revealing how Mn incorporation accelerates Ir oxidation and Ir-O covalency evolution to promote lattice-oxygen activation.

item.title: Inside Back Cover: Neural Engineering Tailored by Molecular Motors With Self‐Reporting for Neuron Activation and Depression Treatment
item.description: In Research Article e2883647, Yang Tian, Limin Zhang, and co-workers report MM-VSD1, a light-driven molecular motor coupled to a near-infrared voltage reporter. It activates mechanosensitive TRPV1 channels in hippocampal neurons, evokes calcium influx and action potentials, and alleviates depression-like behaviours in mice. By bridging mechanical manipulation with functional readouts, this work opens an avenue for mechano-based therapeutic interventions.

item.title: Resurrecting Robust CYP152 Peroxygenases for Versatile Biocatalysis
item.description:
ASR of CYP152 peroxygenases generated reconstructed variants with a shift from hydroxylation in variants further from CYP152L1 to decarboxylation in those closer to CYP152L1. Three thermostable reconstructed variants tolerant to solvents, H2O2, extreme pH, and accepting non-native substrates were obtained. CYP152-AncG2 can catalyze one-pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions and serve as a template for directed evolution. X-ray structure and MD simulations of CYP152-AncG2 indicate that its longer loops, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels are key for enabling its superior features.


ABSTRACT

Cytochrome P450 CYP152s are attractive biocatalysts which catalyze decarboxylation and hydroxylation of fatty acids using H2O2 as a co-substrate (peroxygenase activity). Contemporary CYP152s have limited stability and substrate scope. Here we characterized eight reconstructed variants of CYP152 obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR). The results showed that variants remote from Jeotgalicoccus sp. 8456 (CYP152L1) in the tree used for the ASR tended to catalyze hydroxylation, while nodes closer to CYP152L1 favored decarboxylation; this transition correlates with Q85H substitution and FG-loop insertion alongside other structural features. Three reconstructed variants exhibit high T m (66°C–76°C), tolerance to solvents, H2O2, extreme pH, and use non-native substrates. CYP152-AncG2 can catalyze one-pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions to synthesize methoxy stilbene and can serve as a template for directed evolution. X-ray structure at 1.83 Å and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicate that loop structures, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels in CYP152-AncG2 are key for enabling its superior features. These findings provide insights into the structural and evolutionary features of robust peroxygenase templates for expanding peroxygenase biocatalysis.

item.title: Structure‐Guided Design of Pepper‐Binding Fluorophores Through Hydrogen‐Bonding Engineering
item.description:
We develop a hydrogen-bonding engineering strategy to optimize HBC and HBC620 fluorophores for the Pepper RNA aptamer, creating MBC and PBC620 with drastically improved affinity, cellular brightness, and photostability to support real-time live-cell RNA tracking.


ABSTRACT

Pepper fluorescent RNAs (FRs) enable spatiotemporal imaging of intracellular RNA with high resolution. Although spectral optimization of the HBC scaffold has extended coverage from cyan to red, systematic refinement of binding affinity, photostability, and brightness remains largely unexplored. We describe a hydrogen-bonding strategy that strengthens fluorophore-aptamer interactions by incorporating hydroxyl groups or polyethylene glycol (PEG) moieties into HBC derivatives. The resulting compounds, MBC and PBC620, bind Pepper over 6-fold and 10-fold more tightly than their parent dyes HBC and HBC620, respectively, and exhibit correspondingly higher signal-to-noise ratios and enhanced photostability, with 2.1-fold and 1.5-fold increases in cellular brightness. Molecular models reveal that improved affinity stems from optimally positioned hydrogen bonds with RNA nucleotides. MBC enables real-time tracking of genomic loci with enhanced contrast compared to standard HBC. This work establishes structure-guided interface engineering as a general strategy for improving fluorescent RNA systems.

item.title: Atmosphere‐Dependent Encapsulation and Dewetting in Au/ZnO: A Transient‐Overlayer Strategy for Maximizing Metal‐Support Interfacial Catalysis
item.description:
Redox-driven SMSI dynamics in Au/ZnO drive a transient encapsulation–alloying–dewetting cycle that reconstructs the interface, yielding an expanded metal-support interfacial perimeter. The cycled catalyst exhibits enhanced CO oxidation activity and sintering resistance relative to the fresh counterpart, demonstrating that a transient overlayer can serve as a precursor for interface-engineered catalysis.


ABSTRACT

The strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) has traditionally been viewed as a static phenomenon that modulates catalysis through site blocking. Here, we challenge this classical view by demonstrating that SMSI in Au/ZnO is an atmosphere-dependent dynamic process that can be harnessed to engineer catalytic interfaces. Using in situ transmission electron microscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we track the structural evolution of the Au/ZnO interface throughout redox cycles and reaction conditions. Under H2, oxygen vacancy formation triggers ZnOx encapsulation, followed by AuZn alloying at elevated temperature, which induces nanoparticle reconstruction and expands the metal-support interfacial area. Upon exposure to O2, the alloy decomposes, and the ZnOx overlayer dewets into nanoislands, with some regions undergoing complete retraction. Under CO oxidation conditions, the fully encapsulated state is lost, yet the H2-pretreated catalyst exhibits superior activity and stability. This enhancement arises from alloying-induced interface reconstruction together with residual ZnO nanoislands that persist after dewetting, creating an enlarged and highly active metal–oxide interface. Our work demonstrates a transient-overlayer strategy for catalyst design, in which a pre-formed SMSI layer serves as a precursor that, through controlled redox cycling or reaction conditions, transforms into a high-interface area, sintering-resistant catalytic architecture, thereby transcending the classical encapsulation-activity dilemma.

item.title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
item.description:
Integrating porphyrin into a sulfur-rich benzotrithiophene–thiophene conjugated polymer creates a chemically diversified redox framework for sodium dual-ion storage. Compared with the reference polymer BTB, porphyrin-integrated BTTP enables complementary anion/cation compensation by regulating local electronic environments, thereby enhancing the accessibility of intrinsic multielectron redox chemistry.


ABSTRACT

Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high-energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur-rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state-dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g−1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g−1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g−1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur-rich backbone cooperatively provide potential-dependent coordination environments for PF6 − anions and Na+ cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion-interaction environments within multi-active-unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

item.title: Boron‐Oxygen Covalent Fusion Enables Narrowband Deep‐Red CP‐OLEDs Based on BODIPY Emitters
item.description:
Boron–oxygen covalent fusion enables the first solution-processed narrowband deep-red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence organic light-emitting diodes, delivering a 34 nm full width at half maximum, a |g EL| up to 5.49 × 10−3 and CIE coordinates approaching the NTSC red standard.


ABSTRACT

Realizing solution-processable deep-red circularly polarized organic light-emitting diodes (CP-OLEDs) with both intense CP and high color purity remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report the first solution-processed narrowband deep-red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence OLEDs based on a helically chiral boron-dipyrromethene emitter. Intramolecular boron–oxygen (B–O) covalent fusion simultaneously regulates molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, thereby suppressing excited-state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling while preserving efficient deep-red emission. As a result, BDP-BO exhibits deep-red emission at 654 nm with a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 71% and an ultranarrow emission bandwidth of 34 nm (0.10 eV). The corresponding P- and M-enantiomers display excellent chiroptical activity, with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (|g lum|) up to 3.54 × 10−3 and a circularly polarized luminescence brightness (B CPL) of 49 M−1 cm−1. Exploiting these merits, the M-BDP-BO-based device delivers deep-red electroluminescence (EL) within the National Television System Committee color gamut, a maximum external quantum efficiency of 2.6%, and a large EL dissymmetry factor (|g EL|) of 5.49 × 10−3. This work establishes B–O covalent fusion as an effective strategy for simultaneously regulating molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, providing a versatile platform for high-performance solution-processed deep-red CP-OLEDs.

item.title: π‐Extended Bisallyls Through Valence Isomerism: From Transient Diradicals to Persistent Anions
item.description:
π-Extension brings the hidden bisallyl intermediates of allene dimerization within thermal reach. NMR exchange and calculations identify transient open-shell singlet diradicals, while reduction reverses the valence-isomer preference and stabilizes persistent ring-opened anions through charge-controlled covalent-bond reorganization.


ABSTRACT

Bisallyl diradicals are central intermediates in allene dimerization, yet they are normally too short-lived to observe under thermal conditions. Here, π-extension of Staudinger-type allene dimers weakens the central cyclobutane bond sufficiently to make reversible ring opening accessible near room temperature. Variable-temperature NMR spectroscopy and ROESY exchange correlations reveal repeated cleavage and reformation of this bond, with activation free energies of 15.77 and 13.79 kcal mol−1 for the Staudinger dimer and its π-expanded analogue, respectively. Calculations reproduce this trend and identify low-population open-shell singlet bisallyls as the intermediates, while explaining the absence of neutral-state EPR signals. Reduction reverses the relative stability of the closed and open valence isomers. Voltammetry and chemical reduction support a sequence of ring-opened radical-anion, dianion, and tetraanion states. The dianion is characterized by NMR spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction, while spectroscopy and calculations reveal progressive bond redistribution from mixed-valence allyl-radical/allyl-anion character to two allyl-anion units and, finally, four fluorenyl-anion-like termini. These results connect hidden neutral diradicals with persistent reduced bisallyl frameworks through charge-controlled covalent-bond reorganization.

item.title: Fluorinated Fullerene Derivatives for Thermally Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
item.description:
A new type of fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, were designed to reduce the self-aggregation of phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM). Intermolecular interactions and steric hindrance can improve the microscopic aggregation of fullerenes, enhance the uniformity and stability of the electron transport layer (ETL), and strengthen electron transport. The optimized devices achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.42%, with excellent stability under continuous illumination and high-temperature operation.


ABSTRACT

PCBM (phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester) is one of the most used electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, PCBM tends to self-aggregate during the thermal aging process, disrupting film continuity and limiting device lifetime. To address this issue, we synthesized new fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, forming a composite fullerene ETL by blending with PCBM. We found that fullerene self-aggregation was suppressed through the synergistic effects of weak interactions, such as π–π conjugation between phenyl and fluorophenyl groups and C─H···F van der Waals interactions, and the constrained molecular conformation induced by intermolecular steric hindrance, thereby markedly improving film uniformity and thermal stability, reducing defect-state density, and suppressing ion migration. In addition, the energy level alignment between perovskite and ETL is optimized, enhancing electron transport. Ultimately, 5FPCPB, having more compatible energy levels and stronger conjugation effects than FPCPB, achieved a 26.42% power conversion efficiency (PCE), with improved operational and thermal stability (T90 under light = 1200 h; T95 under 85°C > 700 h). The fullerene co-doping strategy opens a new pathway for achieving high-performance and thermally stable perovskite devices.

item.title: Mechanistic Insights Into the Solid‐State Redox Reactions: Role of Organic Piezoelectric Materials
item.description:
Crystal symmetry powers chemistry: Non-centrosymmetric organic piezoelectric crystals convert mechanical energy into electrical polarization, enabling solid-state redox reactions under ball milling. In contrast, chemically identical centrosymmetric crystal forms remain largely inactive. This symmetry-dependent reactivity enables C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P bonds formation, establishing crystal symmetry as a powerful design principle for sustainable mechanochemical synthesis.


ABSTRACT

Mechanochemistry has gained tremendous recent attention because it combines sustainability with the ability to access unique reaction pathways and materials while offering practical advantages for efficient and scalable chemical synthesis. However, predicting solid-state transformations from mechanical energy remains a formidable challenge, as the current mechanistic models are insufficient. While solid-state electrocatalytic reactions in the presence of inorganic piezoelectric materials have been demonstrated recently, the ability of piezoelectric organic solids, which possess an order of magnitude lower piezoelectric coefficients, remain completely unexplored. Here, using different crystalline forms, we demonstrate that under ball-milling, non-centrosymmetric organic crystals generate piezoelectric potentials that are sufficient to drive a range of redox bond-forming reactions, including C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P couplings. To further evaluate the role of piezoelectricity, we compared chemically identical crystal forms of a compound, differing only in symmetry: Non-centrosymmetric crystals are highly reactive, whereas centrosymmetric counterparts remain largely inert. These findings reveal crystal symmetry as a previously unrecognized determinant of chemical function and identify organic piezoelectric solids as active energy-transduction media for chemical synthesis. More broadly, this work provides a framework for designing self-powered chemical systems that directly couple mechanical energy harvesting with molecular transformation.

item.title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
item.description:
A Keplerate, an inorganic, porous buckyball was used as a host for copper metal cations ligated by histidine surrogates. Prepared by a simple assembly technique, the guest–host complex was used as a primitive biomimetic model of a monooxygenase enzyme complex, where C─H bonds were electrocatalytically hydroxylated by oxygen under reducing conditions. The confined space at the catalytic site yielded rate accelerations of two-orders of magnitude.


ABSTRACT

Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for CuII. The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

item.title: Oxidative‐Branch Engineering for Radical Regulation in Methane‐to‐Methanol Photocatalysis
item.description:
Selective methane-to-methanol photocatalysis requires a radical environment that activates methane while suppressing methanol overoxidation. Engineering the oxidative ZnO branch of an In2O3/ZnO S-scheme heterojunction regulates this environment, delivering methanol at 638.2 µmol g−1 h−1 with 93.8% selectivity. Methanol selectivity is governed by a kinetic balance between productive oxidation and overoxidation, rather than by radical maximization.


ABSTRACT

Selective methane-to-methanol photocatalysis requires efficient methane activation and control over the radical environment that determines whether methanol is preserved or further oxidized. Radical generation is therefore double-edged: an underdeveloped radical environment limits C–H activation and methanol-forming oxygenation, whereas an excessive oxidative environment promotes secondary oxidation. Here, the radical environment is regulated by engineering the oxidative branch of an In2O3/ZnO S-scheme heterojunction. Under ambient-pressure gas–solid flow conditions with O2 and H2O as co-reactants, the optimized catalyst delivers methanol at 638.2 µmol g−1 h−1 with 93.8% selectivity. The volcano-shaped dependence of methanol productivity on ZnO loading shows that methanol accumulation is governed by competition between partial and deep oxidation rather than oxidative strength alone. Spectroscopic analyses support an S-scheme charge-transfer pathway that preserves oxidative holes on ZnO and reductive electrons on In2O3, coupling methane activation, water oxidation and O2 reduction within a branch-specific redox network. Increasing ZnO loading strengthens the methyl-, superoxide- and hydroxyl-radical probe responses, whereas methanol selectivity peaks at an intermediate loading. At higher ZnO loading, deep-oxidation signatures emerge without further enhancement of methanol-related surface chemistry, whereas the optimized heterojunction maintains a formation-dominant surface pathway. These findings identify a kinetic balance in the radical environment, rather than radical maximization, as the selectivity principle for methane-to-methanol photocatalysis.

item.title: Zeshi Li
item.description:
“When I was a kid I wanted to be a scientist, assuming that scientists build super-robots; but I became one that builds molecules… If I were a piece of lab equipment I would be a microscope because I would get to see both the “bigger picture” and important details…”

item.title: An Ether‐Chain‐Functionalized Zwitterion Enables Mild Zinc‐Ion Coordination and Dual‐Site Polyiodide Capture in Aqueous Zinc–Iodine Batteries
item.description:
An ether-chain-functionalized zwitterion couples mild Zn2+ coordination with reversible dual-site polyiodide capture. Imidazolium-induced electrostatic repulsion facilitates Zn2+ dissociation and uniform deposition, while complementary electrostatic and ion–dipole interactions suppress polyiodide shuttling, enabling Zn–I2 cells to sustain >35 000 cycles and 300 mAh pouch cells to operate stably for >1200 cycles.


ABSTRACT

Aqueous zinc–iodine batteries are limited by zinc dendrite growth at the anode and polyiodide shuttling at the cathode. Conventional strongly coordinating additives can regulate Zn2+ solvation, but the resulting high ligand-dissociation barrier impedes interfacial charge transfer, creating an inherent trade-off between solvation regulation and reaction kinetics. Here, we introduce ZEG, an ether-chain-functionalized imidazolium sulfonate zwitterion that combines mild Zn2+ coordination with dual-site polyiodide capture. In ZEG, the imidazolium cation reduces the donor strength of the ether oxygens through electron-withdrawing and further weakens ether-chain coordination by electrostatically repelling Zn2+, thereby lowering the ligand-dissociation barrier while preserving solvation-shell regulation. Meanwhile, at the iodine cathode, the imidazolium cation and ether chain provide complementary sites that reversibly capture polyiodides through electrostatic attraction and ion–dipole interactions, respectively, thereby suppressing polyiodide shuttling and improving iodine utilization. With ZEG, Zn–I2 full cells sustain over 35,000 cycles at 10 A g−1, while 300 mAh pouch cells with a high iodine loading of 30 mg cm−2 operate stably for over 1200 cycles. By integrating mild Zn2+ coordination with reversible dual-site polyiodide capture, this design reconciles solvation regulation with rapid interfacial charge transfer and offers an innovative molecular design principle for multifunctional electrolyte additives.

item.title: Chalcogen‐Bridge‐Regulated Proton Shuttling in Tantalum‐Doped Ruthenium Oxide for Robust Acidic Water Oxidation
item.description:
The in-situ Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XPS, x-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES), and pH-dependent electrochemical tests support the bridge atoms in Ta─X─RuO2 strongly affect the proton shuttle during acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER).


ABSTRACT

The acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) kinetics on ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) is fundamentally restricted by sluggish deprotonation and interfacial proton transfer. Herein, we introduce chalcogen atoms to tantalum doped RuO2 (Ta─X─RuO2, X = O, S, Se, and Te) and reveal its effects on proton shuttling, including deprotonation and proton transfer from electrocatalyst surface to bulk electrolyte. Significantly, Ta─S─RuO2 exhibits optimized OER performance due to the balanced hydrogen binding strength of bridge sulfur atoms, promoting deprotonation kinetics and modulating the interfacial water structure to form flexible hydrogen bond network for accelerated proton transfer. Only 1.89 V is demanded for Ta─S─RuO2 to reach 3 A cm−2 geo and maintains robust performance for 1000 h with voltage decay of 49.0 µV h−1 stemming from the efficient hydrogen bond network to lower the local H+ concentration, suppressing the overoxidation of Ru. This work not only reports a novel high-performance Ta─X─RuO2 electrocatalysts for acidic OER but also provides new insight into chalcogen-regulated proton shuttling and promoted OER kinetics and stability, offering guidance to the design of future generation RuO2-based electrocatalyst.

item.title: Transformer‐Guided Co‐Optimization of Mutation Prioritization and Thermodynamic Probe Design for Mutation Detection
item.description:
An iterative computational panel design framework in which biological mutation relevance and chemical probe discriminability are jointly optimized. Mutation attribution and population frequency prioritize biologically relevant targets, while MUT/WT binding free-energy differences (ΔΔG°) guide probe design. The resulting 8-plex assay enables sensitive mutation enrichment and detection down to 0.03% VAF.


ABSTRACT

The design of sequence-selective DNA probes has long been limited by a decoupled workflow in which target selection proceeds without considering the physicochemical determinants of probe performance, such as thermodynamic stability and mismatch discrimination. Here, we establish an iterative computational design strategy that unifies mutation prioritization with chemical probe design. A custom transformer model extracts diagnostic attribution scores of mutations from 1,782 samples, generating semantic maps to guide probe placement. Candidate designs undergo in silico thermodynamic screening based on differential binding free energy. Probes failing to satisfy the integrated criteria of thermodynamic discrimination, diagnostic attribution, and population frequency are further evaluated by refining their spatial configuration to co-optimize thermodynamic discriminability and clinical relevance. This iterative process converges on an 8-plex targeted panel. Wet laboratory validation confirms 0.03% variant allele frequency detection with low assay cost and short turnaround time. Clinical testing on 375 samples achieves AUROC values of 0.96 for tissue and 0.90 for plasma. This work provides a potential chemical framework for nucleic acid probe design that could be explored in other molecular diagnostic systems.

item.title: Strategies for Preparing Migration‐Resistant Macromolecular Antioxidants
item.description:
A well-defined “3C principle” covering compatibility, cocrystallization, and crosslinking was proposed for constructing macromolecular antioxidants with superior stability, which were prepared through ring-opening metathesis polymerization or free radical-type copolymerization.


ABSTRACT

Polymeric materials are susceptible to thermo-oxidative degradation during melt processing and usage, which can be prevented using antioxidants. However, conventional small-molecule antioxidants, such as phenolic antioxidants, are prone to migration, which compromises their long-term effectiveness. To address this, for crystalline/semicrystalline polymers, we propose a systematic design strategy for macromolecular antioxidants based on the “3C principle” (Compatibility, cocrystallization, and crosslinking) to construct novel stabilizers with enhanced antioxidant performance and migration resistance. For noncrystalline polymers, macromolecular antioxidants satisfying only two of these criteria can also provide good antioxidant performance. Based on these design principles, three different types of macromolecular antioxidants were developed with structures tailored to the characteristics of commodity plastics, including polyethylene, polymethyl methacrylate, and polystyrene. This work provides a new approach for enhancing the service stability of polymeric materials and offers a broad molecular design strategy for functionalized polymer materials.

item.title: Carbonyl‐Rich Polyimide Covalent Organic Frameworks as Anode Coating for Uniform Sodium Deposition
item.description:
Two isocyanate-based, carbonyl-rich 2D PI COFs were newly synthesized and employed as artificial anode coatings for sodium metal batteries to enhance battery stability. Among them, the TATT-NTCDA-COF-based full cell exhibited stable cycling for over 1390 cycles at 5 C and retained >90% capacity after 750 cycles at 10 C.


ABSTRACT

Two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs), by virtue of their structural diversity, high specific surface area, and facile functionalization, have emerged as a promising anode coating for sodium metal batteries (SMBs). Herein, we report two polyimide COFs (TATT-NTCDA‑COF and TATT-PMDA‑COF) constructed from isocyanurate-based amine building blocks, which feature profuse ion-binding active sites and a robust, ordered framework, thereby significantly enhancing ion transport, fostering uniform sodium deposition, and suppressing dendrite growth. Benefiting from this unique design and its reliable stability, the symmetric cell based on TATT-NTCDA‑COF operates stably for over 1200 h at 0.1 mA cm−2. When assembled into a full cell with a commercial Na3V2(PO4)3 (NVP) cathode, it delivers an initial discharge capacity of 107.4 mAh g−1, retains 9.3% capacity after 800 cycles at 1 C, and maintains over 90% capacity retention even after 1390 cycles at 5 C and 750 cycles at 10 C. Thus, the rational design of carbonyl-rich 2D COFs is of great significance for the construction of artificial anode coatings for SMBs.

item.title: Organocatalytic Enantiodifferentiation of Two Aryl Groups with Similar Steric Hindrances: Construction of gem‐Diaryl Acyclic Quaternary Stereocenters
item.description:
A phase-transfer catalyst enabled enantiodifferentiation of two aryl groups with similar steric hindrances via diaryl conjugated carbanion intermediates has been developed. A variety of gem-diaryl compounds bearing acyclic all-carbon quaternary stereocenters were synthesized in high yields and excellent enantioselectivities.


ABSTRACT

Enantiodifferentiation of two aryl groups with similar steric hindrances is challenging. Although reactions involving diaryl ketones, diaryl alkenes, diaryl imines, diaryl carbenes, and diaryl radicals as substrates or intermediates have been reported for this purpose, successful enantiodifferentiation via diaryl conjugated carbanion intermediates has yet to be achieved. Moreover, existing methodologies predominantly rely on transition-metal catalysis and are largely limited to the construction of gem-diaryl tertiary stereocenters, with no examples reported for the construction of gem-diaryl acyclic quaternary stereocenters. In this study, we have developed a phase-transfer catalyst enabled enantiodifferentiation of two aryl groups with similar steric hindrances via diaryl conjugated carbanion intermediates. With this new approach, a variety of gem-diaryl compounds bearing acyclic all-carbon quaternary stereocenters were synthesized in high yields and excellent enantioselectivities.

item.title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Cross‐Coupling of Transiently Stable Heterocyclic Organolithiums
item.description:
Fast coupling outcompetes organolithium decomposition. Catalyst benchmarking enables transient pyridyl, quinolyl, indazolyl, and related organolithiums to participate in the Murahashi coupling, while continuous-flow generation extends the approach to reagents too unstable for conventional batch handling.


ABSTRACT

The use of organolithium reagents in cross-coupling (the Murahashi coupling) has undergone a resurgence over the past decade, driven by the discovery that modern ligands and catalysts can promote productive couplings that outcompete common side reactions. Despite this progress, most reported methods rely on stable, well-behaved organolithium partners such as n-BuLi and PhLi, leaving many synthetically valuable but highly sensitive heterocyclic organolithiums outside the practical scope. In this work, we employ high-throughput experimentation (HTE) to identify catalytic systems that enable C─C bond formation on minute or sub-minute time scales. These ultrafast conditions enable coupling of sensitive organolithium species, such as lithiated pyridines and quinolines, before they decompose under conventional cross-coupling conditions. We identify several complementary, top-performing catalyst systems that address the different challenges encountered across nucleophile–electrophile combinations, including catalyst inhibition, side reactions, and rapid organolithium decomposition. Limits of the batch protocol are identified and overcome through development of an alternative flash-chemistry protocol that further expands the scope to organolithium reagents that decompose on time scales of seconds. Together, these studies establish a practical strategy for coupling transient heterocyclic organolithiums and substantially expand the scope of the Murahashi reaction.

item.title: Phenonium‐Ion‐Mediated Skeletal Editing of Paracyclophanes
item.description:
Phenonium-ion chemistry enables the modular skeletal editing of paracyclophanes. Regioselective nucleophilic trapping expands one or both aliphatic bridges, enables iterative access to higher paracyclophane homologues, and translates bridge topology into a functional design parameter, as demonstrated with a bridge-expanded TADF emitter.


ABSTRACT

Phenonium ions have played a central role in physical–organic chemistry, yet their use as strategic intermediates in synthesis remains underexplored. Here, we report a phenonium-ion-mediated strategy for the skeletal editing of paracyclophanes. Installation of a one-carbon handle at the aliphatic bridge, followed by direct alcohol activation with BF3·OEt2 under solvolysis-avoiding conditions, generates a paracyclophane-derived phenonium ion that undergoes regioselective ring opening by external nucleophiles. This strategy provides modular access to functionalized higher paracyclophane homologues and tolerates S-, N-, C-, selenium-, and halide-based nucleophiles under operationally simple, gram-scalable conditions. The sequence can be applied iteratively and extended to double bridge expansion, while reductive desulfurization furnishes the corresponding parent hydrocarbons. Mechanistic studies combining nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, kinetic analysis, stereochemical probes, and density functional theory calculations support a self-accelerating mechanism in which product water shifts BF3 speciation toward BF3·H2O, which assists leaving-group departure through hydrogen-bond donation and thereby facilitates phenonium-ion formation. Together, these results establish paracyclophane-derived phenonium ions as controllable intermediates for skeletal editing and provide practical access to higher paracyclophane topologies with application potential in functional materials, as exemplified by a bridge-expanded thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) emitter.

item.title: 3D Electron Diffraction Reveals Counterion Coordination in Co‐Existing Polymorphs of Ag29 Nanocluster
item.description:
By combining in situ drop-casting with 3D electron diffraction, the co-existing cubic (“squeeze”) and trigonal (“trap”) polymorphs of the [Ag29(BDT)12(TPP)4]3− nanocluster were resolved crystal-by-crystal. Difference electrostatic potential maps localized elusive Na+ counterions, revealing how macroscopic crystal packing directly relates to distinct nanoscale coordination environments.


ABSTRACT

We unravel the complete structural architecture of the polymorphic Na3[Ag29(BDT)12(TPP)4] nanocluster (NC) using three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) of microscopic crystals. By drop-casting nanocluster solution directly onto microscopy grids, we achieve in situ crystallization of nanometer-sized polymorphs and independently resolve co-existing cubic and trigonal phases crystal-by-crystal from a single grid square. Using difference electrostatic potential (DESP) maps derived from empirical 3D ED data, we pinpoint the specific lattice locations of the elusive Na+ counterions and observe distinct coordination environments across the two polymorphs. In the densely packed, solvent-free cubic phase, Na+ binds exclusively to thermodynamically favored pockets formed by one core-anchored and two staple sulfur atoms. Conversely, within the open, solvated trigonal lattice, Na+ occupies both these core-anchored sites and alternative positions coordinated entirely by three sulfur atoms of an outer Ag3S3 staple motif. These findings establish 3D ED as a powerful tool for resolving nanoscale polymorphic mixtures and demonstrate how macroscopic crystal packing influences local ionic interactions, providing key structural insights for the design of cluster-based assemblies.

item.title: Catalysis on a Knife's Edge: Detailed Mechanistic Studies Reveal a Fine Balance Between Catalyst Deactivation and Productive Reactivity in CuH‐Catalyzed Alkene Hydrofunctionalization
item.description:
A combination of kinetic, structural, and computational experiments from Ginovska, Raugei, Tran, and coworkers has offered detailed insight into bisphosphine-ligated copper hydride speciation and deactivation mechanisms. These studies provide a valuable blueprint for the further advancement of copper hydride catalysis through new ligand designs.


ABSTRACT

Copper hydride catalyst systems have been widely applied to the hydrofunctionalization of unsaturated compounds, enabling the synthesis of a range of valuable organic products. In particular, copper catalysts supported by bulky bisphosphine ligands such as DTBM-SEGPHOS have enjoyed noteworthy success across a range of substrate classes, with the highly unstable monomeric LCuH (L = DTBM-SEGPHOS) often implicated as the active form of the catalyst. Recently, Ryan et al. Angewandte Chemie Novit 2, no. 2 (2026): e70025 have not only characterized the elusive monomeric LCuH, but have provided a suite of kinetic and computational experiments that reveal the mechanisms by which these catalysts form inactive higher order Cu aggregates. Collectively, these important studies substantially increase knowledge of LCuH speciation and the factors that control the relative rates between productive alkene hydrocupration and catalyst deactivation—insights which are anticipated to inform the design of next-generation catalysts.

item.title: Outside Front Cover: Light‐Driven Out‐of‐Equilibrium Helicity Control in a Diarylethene–Helicene Photosystem (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 45/2026)
item.description: In the Research Article e5252700, Eric Sidler, Ben L. Feringa, and co-workers report a molecular energy ratchet driven by light. Photochemical ring closure enables rapid helix inversion toward the thermodynamically favoured state, while subsequent ring opening kinetically traps the acquired helicity. This sequence drives a diarylethene–[5]helicene photoswitch away from equilibrium, providing directional and persistent control over molecular helicity.

item.title: Inside Front Cover: Modulated Structure‐Electronic Coupling at Pt/CeOx–TiO2 Interfaces Boosts Low‐Temperature Preferential CO Oxidation (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 45/2026)
item.description: Engineering distinct Pt–O–Ti and Pt–O–Ce interfacial motifs under H2-rich conditions enables preferential CO oxidation while suppressing competing H2 oxidation. Hydrogen activation at Pt–O–Ti modulates the electronic state of Pt and weakens CO binding, while Pt–O–Ce facilitates CO oxidation, together directing catalytic reactivity toward highly selective CO removal from hydrogen-rich streams. More in the Research Article e7158452, Akhil Tayal, Anatoly I. Frenkel, WooChul Jung, Hyun You Kim, and co-workers.

item.title: Outside Back Cover: Synthesis of Aminocyclopropanes by Redox‐Neutral Aminoalkylation (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 45/2026)
item.description: In the Communication e8092854, Nuno Maulide and co-workers present a redox-neutral hydroaminoalkylation enabling access to aminocyclopropanes. This method utilizes a bench-stable hemiaminal and showcases a solvolysis-only activation, thus allowing broad substrate tolerance and orthogonality to traditional methods. A one-pot variant and pharmacological studies to demonstrate the power of aminocyclopropanes as bioisosteres for gem-alpha-dimethylamines further exemplify the utility of this work.

item.title: Heme Peroxo Reaction Intermediates: Mimicking Biological Structure and Reactivity With Synthetic Model Systems
item.description:
Despite the traditional classification as sluggish oxidants, heme peroxo intermediates have recently emerged into the spotlight as terminal oxidants in a medley of significant heme enzymes. A clear mechanistic comprehension of those enzymes is lacking, notwithstanding their growing relevance in human disease and therapy. Meticulously designed model compounds have shed pivotal insight into these reaction landscapes, albeit with key unknowns still exist.


ABSTRACT

Heme enzymes are at the center of a mélange of salient transformations in biology, and for aerobic life, dioxygen binding and activation are by far the most critical. These enzymes typically channel through a panel of distinct heme-oxygen adducts, of which early- or mid-valent (i.e., Fe(III)-containing) intermediates have long remained underexplored. These ferric heme-oxygen intermediates demonstrate highly versatile chemistries, making the detailed comprehension of their chemistries a challenging endeavor. Intriguingly, however, systems with climacteric mid-valent intermediates have rapidly acquired interest in therapeutic applications, predominantly owing to their implications in human pathogenesis and prognosis. This review presents a comprehensive overview of mechanistic propositions for enzymes with heme-peroxo active species, and the key contributions from synthetic model compounds that have shed light on crucial subtleties geared toward a clear understanding of those biological pathways. Critical aspects of primary and secondary coordination spheres that directly assist in orchestrating the remarkably versatile reactivity attributes of heme peroxo complexes are also discussed. Most significantly, despite 40 years of interrogation, a crucial body of ambiguities pertaining to heme peroxo intermediates still remains to this day, warranting further in-depth biological surveying as well as meticulously designed bona fide functional model systems.

item.title: Beyond Nature's Blueprint: Macrocyclic Peptides Containing Unnatural Amino Acids in Therapeutic Development
item.description:
Strategic incorporation of unnatural amino acids transforms macrocyclic peptides into drug-like molecules capable of engaging challenging targets. These building blocks enhance stability, permeability, and bioavailability, accelerating the development of next-generation peptide therapeutics.


ABSTRACT

Macrocyclic peptides have emerged as a compelling class of therapeutics, combining the modularity and synthetic accessibility of small molecules with the high affinity and target selectivity of biologics. Their ability to engage challenging and traditionally “undruggable” protein targets—including protein–protein interactions and allosteric sites—has generated widespread interest. However, pharmacokinetic limitations such as poor oral bioavailability, metabolic instability, and low membrane permeability continue to hinder clinical translation. The strategic incorporation of unnatural amino acids (UAAs) has proven critical for overcoming these challenges, enabling fine-tuning of key physicochemical and pharmacological properties. In this review, we highlight recent clinical advances—including motixafortide and zilucoplan—and examine how UAAs are deployed to optimize drug-like characteristics across diverse therapeutic areas. We discuss emerging strategies, illustrative case studies, and design principles that collectively support the development of next-generation macrocyclic peptide drugs.

item.title: Chirality‐Matched Piezoelectric Responsiveness and Energy Transfer in Supramolecular Co‐Assembly of Dipeptides
item.description:
Homochirality is a hallmark of living systems, enabling precise molecular recognition and cellular homeostasis. This study explores its role in synthetic supramolecular nanomaterials through dipeptide co-assemblies. Homochiral assemblies form fibrillar networks, whereas heterochiral systems produce short-range fibrillar structures. Chirality-matched π–π stacking in homochiral assemblies enhances energy transfer and piezoelectric properties, highlighting the functional preference for homochirality.


ABSTRACT

The concept of homochirality is fundamental to living systems, where biopolymers exhibit a uniform chiral signature. The absence of heterochiral or racemic biopolymers in nature highlights the importance of homochirality in precise molecular recognition, efficient packing, and controlled folding for maintaining cellular homeostasis and biological function. However, the role of homochirality in governing emergent functional properties in synthetic supramolecular nanomaterials has been less explored. Here, we investigate homochiral recognition of dipeptides at their co-assembled state. Homochiral peptides on co-assembly form supramolecular gels, whereas heterochiral peptides fail to gelify. Co-assembly of homochiral peptides results in the formation of long-range fibrillar network with high aspect ratios, while co-assembly of heterochiral peptides produces short-range, discrete morphology. Computational insight further reveals that dipeptides containing similar chiral α-amino acids promote efficient molecular packing and long-range π–π stacking, whereas dipeptides with opposite chirality disrupt these interactions, leading to short-range assembly. The preference for like-like interactions in homochiral co-assemblies has been explored through FRET and piezoelectric measurements. Homochiral assembly exhibits significantly higher energy-transfer efficiency and enhanced piezoelectric properties than heterochiral assembly. Overall, this study highlights the fundamental concept of homochirality in nature and its relationship with emergent functional properties.

item.title: Orthosteric Control of Acidity Through Sulfate Binding in a Neutral Cyclo[8]pyrrole
item.description:
A neutral naphthalimide-fused cyclo[8]pyrrole combines amplified NH acidity with strong sulfate binding. Persistent orthosteric association of sulfate raises the first apparent pK a by nearly four units, converting anion recognition into direct regulation of Brønsted acidity without changing covalent structure, redox state, or solvent.


ABSTRACT

Acid–base equilibria can be shifted when binding events alter the local electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding environment of an ionizable site. Implementing such binding-linked acidity changes in a discrete synthetic system would enable regulation of proton activity without changing molecular composition or solvent. Here we describe a new naphthalimide-fused analogue of cyclo[8]pyrrole in which anion recognition dramatically shifts protonation equilibria. Whereas established cyclo[8]pyrroles preferentially form globally aromatic dications, the electron-deficient macrocycle shows an unusual preference for a persistent neutral redox state, while simultaneously revealing exceptionally high Brønsted acidity in organic solvents. The neutral macrocycle retains key anion-recognition characteristics of dicationic cyclo[8]pyrroles, including strong sulfate affinity. Sulfate binding increases the effective first pK a in DMSO by roughly four units, providing an orthosteric, anion-actuated acid switch and expanding the design space of switchable acidity beyond host–guest pK a shifts and light-addressable photoacids.

item.title: Small Molecule Modulation of TERRA RNA Quadruplex Reprograms ALT‐Telomere Maintenance
item.description:
The telomeric lncRNA TERRA forms RNA G-quadruplex structures that regulate telomere integrity. An indoloquinoxaline ligand (IQ4) selectively binds and stabilizes the TERRA rG4, disrupts the TERRA–TRF2 interaction, and promotes telomere dysfunction, DNA damage, and antiproliferative effects in ALT-positive cells.


ABSTRACT

Telomeric repeat–containing RNA (TERRA) plays a central role in telomere maintenance in telomerase-negative cancers that employ the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway; however, its RNA G-quadruplex (rG4) structures remain underexplored as chemical targets. Here, we report a structure-guided approach to selectively modulate TERRA rG4 using an indoloquinoxaline-based small-molecule scaffold. Biophysical analyses confirm high-affinity and selective binding, while NMR and computational studies identify terminal tetrad stacking as the dominant binding mode of the ligand to the TERRA rG4. Ligand engagement disrupts the TERRA–Telomeric Repeat-Binding Factor 2 (TRF2) interaction (ELISA, EMSA) and alters TERRA abundance (qRT-PCR). Transcriptomic (RNA-seq) analysis reveals ligand-induced differential expression of ALT-associated genes and DNA metabolism pathways. In ALT-positive U2OS cells, the ligand localizes to the nucleus, induces telomere-associated DNA damage, and triggers S-phase arrest and apoptosis. These findings establish TERRA rG4 as a chemically addressable structural element in ALT biology and demonstrate the potential of small molecules to probe and modulate long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)-mediated genome maintenance.

item.title: Access to Unsupported Iminobismuthane and Tetraazabismole Species Enabled by a Rigid and Bulky Organobismuthinidene
item.description:
By employing a sterically bulky monocoordinate bismuthinidene, the synthesis and characterization of the first examples of an unsupported iminobismuthane and tetraazabismole was achieved via reactions with organic azides. The corresponding amines could be accessed by reduction, leading to the regeneration of the Bi(I) compound. Hence, we also highlight the first example of a catalytic Bi(I)/Bi(III) redox cycle of a monocoordinated bismuthinidene.


ABSTRACT

Herein, we report the reactivity of a monocoordinate bismuthinidene (1) with various organic azides. The reaction of 1 with p-toluenesulfonyl azide resulted in the formation of an unprecedented, unsupported iminobismuthane (2), which features the shortest reported Bi–N distance of 2.041(3) Å in an iminobismuthane. Conversely, the reaction of 1 with 4-azidobiphenyl resulted in the first example of a species containing a tetraazabismole (BiN4) heterocycle (3). We also highlight that 1 demonstrates catalytic activity, enabling the reduction of a selection of organic azides.

item.title: Tailoring and Unraveling Surface Functionalization of Nanomaterials via Self‐Reporting NIR‐Induced Upconversion Energy Transfer Process
item.description:
A three-in-one paradigm for UCNR is established, wherein a single nanostructure concurrently serves as a near-infrared (NIR) light-harvesting antenna, a polymerization substrate, and a self-reporting optical probe. NIR-driven PET-RAFT transforms the invisible surface functionalization into a real-time luminescence readout, realizing a programmable and perceptible light-based paradigm for intelligent self-sensing nanoplatforms.


ABSTRACT

The surface functionalization chemistry of nanomaterials remains a black box, where the dynamic modification process is conventionally imperceptible, which severely limits the rational design of advanced nanohybrids. Herein, a holistic strategy that transforms upconversion nanorods (UCNR) surface functionalization from an empirically treated outcome into an optically self-reporting process via near-infrared (NIR)-mediated photoinduced electron/energy transfer-reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (PET-RAFT) polymerization is present. This three-in-one design, where the UCNR concurrently acts as a NIR-harvesting antenna, polymerization substrate, and optical signaling unit, enables the precise, temporally controlled growth and monitoring of polymer shells with tunable thickness and grafting density. Critically, a linear correlation between the evolving polymer shell architecture and the upconversion luminescence intensity was unraveled, thereby turning the optical signal into a real-time, nondestructive probe that reveals the invisible surface modification process. Building upon this self-monitoring capability, the polymer brushes were further engineered to template the in situ growth of gold nanoparticles, establishing a cascaded energy transfer pathway for efficient photothermal conversion. Using the nanohybrids as a built-in ratiometric fluorescent nanothermometer, the nanohybrid enables real-time temperature feedback during NIR irradiation as precise nanothermometry. This work establishes a new paradigm for creating intelligent, self-sensing nanoplatforms with profound implications for precision theranostics and adaptive photonic materials.

item.title: Beyond Radical Emitters: Hot‐Exciton Electroluminescence From Singlet Diradicaloids
item.description:
The first hot-exciton mechanism in a singlet diradicaloid is demonstrated in a polychlorinated Thiele hydrocarbon-based organic light-emitting transistor. Reverse intersystem crossing involving the T2 and bright singly excited states enables electroluminescence beyond the 25% spin-statistical limit, leading to remarkable external quantum efficiency.


ABSTRACT

Overcoming the 25% spin-statistical limit of fluorescent emitters remains a central challenge in organic electroluminescence. Although radical emitters efficiently harvest doublet excitons in organic light-emitting diodes, their optoelectronic performance can be affected by limited charge-carrier mobility and efficiency roll-off. Here we introduce trityl-based singlet diradicaloids with small diradical character as a new class of open-shell emitters and demonstrate their operation in organic light-emitting transistors (OLETs) using the polychlorinated Thiele hydrocarbon (TTH) as emitter. Comparison with previously reported radical-based devices reveals spin utilization around or exceeding 0.38 in TTH-based OLETs. Time-resolved electroluminescence, fs and ns transient absorption measurements, and quantum-chemical calculations demonstrate that this enhancement does not originate from triplet–triplet annihilation but from hot-exciton mechanism enabled by the diradical electronic structure, where the T2 state efficiently repopulates the emissive singlet via reverse intersystem crossing (RISC). Unlike conventional hot-exciton emitters based on donor–acceptor architectures, this system demonstrates hot-exciton behavior in a singlet diradicaloid framework. Reduced charge trapping further highlights singlet diradicaloids with small diradical character as promising platforms for efficient and stable electroluminescent devices.

item.title: Role of Graphene Oxide in the Nucleation and Growth of Gold Nanoparticles Revealed by Operando Time‐Resolved Studies
item.description:
Graphene oxide accelerates AuCl4 − reduction under irradiation and directs edge-selective nucleation and quasi-one-dimensional organization of gold nanoparticles at oxygen-rich boundaries. Operando SAXS and UV–vis spectroscopy, supported by pulse radiolysis and DFT, reveal how progressive conversion of GO to rGO removes interfacial constraints, shifting nanoparticle evolution from size-limited growth to rapid coalescence.


ABSTRACT

Understanding nanoparticle growth in complex composite systems remains a central challenge in materials chemistry. Herein, we elucidate the stepwise formation mechanism of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) in graphene oxide (GO) aqueous systems under well-defined reductive conditions. Pulse radiolysis reveals that GO significantly accelerates AuCl4 − reduction by hydrated electrons (e aq −), thereby altering early-stage kinetics. Operando synchrotron small-angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) and time-resolved UV–vis absorption spectroscopy enable direct observation of AuNP nucleation and growth. Au(III) reduction precedes GO reduction, and nascent Au clusters preferentially anchor at GO edges through interactions with carboxyl groups, resulting in anisotropic, size-constrained growth. As GO becomes progressively reduced, depletion of oxygen-containing functional groups weakens interfacial stabilization and promotes nanoparticle coalescence. This stepwise mechanism integrates kinetic, spectroscopic, structural, and theoretical evidence, identifying GO as both a kinetic modulator and a spatial growth regulator. The insights provide general design principles for size-controlled nanoparticle growth in graphene-based composite systems.

item.title: Logic‐Gated DNA Cascade Amplification Enables High‐Fidelity Intercellular Communication in Synthetic Protocells
item.description:
A programmable communication framework is reported that integrates logic-gated DNA signal processing with cascade amplification to enable high-fidelity chemical messaging between synthetic sender and receiver protocells. This work provides a versatile strategy for constructing synthetic multicellular networks with enhanced communication fidelity, long-range signaling capability, and programmable downstream responses.


ABSTRACT

Intercellular communication in synthetic protocells is often constrained by passive diffusion, leading to signal attenuation and spurious activation that limit functional outcomes. Here, we report a programmable communication framework that integrates logic-gated DNA signal processing with cascade amplification to enable high-fidelity chemical messaging between synthetic sender and receiver protocells. Sender protocells are equipped with membrane-anchored DNA logic circuits that release a messenger strand only upon dual-input recognition, while receiver protocells decode the transmitted signal through a surface-confined hybridization chain reaction that amplifies the response and suppresses false-positive activation. Beyond information transfer, the amplified signal is converted into functional execution by recruiting a photosensitizer to the receiver membrane, enabling light-triggered modulation of membrane integrity and controlled molecular transport. Together, this logic-controlled and cascade-amplified communication system establishes a signal-to-function transduction pathway in synthetic protocell communities, providing a versatile strategy for constructing synthetic multicellular networks with enhanced communication fidelity, long-range signaling capability, and programmable downstream responses.

item.title: From Stable Radicals to Radical‑Trapping Antioxidants: Blatter Radicals Potently Inhibit Autoxidation and Suppress Ferroptosis
item.description:
Blatter radicals demonstrate unexpected reactivity as radical‑trapping antioxidants (RTAs), inhibiting lipid peroxidation with super‑stoichiometric efficacy. This chemistry confers potent biological applications: anti‑ferroptotic cytoprotection at nanomolar levels, rescue from oxygen‑glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) injury, and anti‑inflammatory effects in vitro.


ABSTRACT

Ferroptosis is a clinically important form of regulated cell death implicated in numerous degenerative pathologies, making the discovery of novel ferroptosis inhibitors of great translational interest. Radical‑trapping antioxidants (RTAs) effectively prevent lipid peroxidation (LPO) and constitute the largest and most important class of ferroptosis inhibitors. However, current approaches for compound discovery and mechanistic studies rely almost exclusively on phenolic or aromatic amine scaffolds, which are typically identified via labor‑intensive high‑throughput screening or adapted from classical antioxidants. Here, we demonstrate that Blatter radicals potently inhibit autoxidation and suppress ferroptosis. Beyond their intrinsic potent radical‑trapping capability, these compounds exhibit super‑stoichiometric activity in inhibiting (phospho)lipid peroxidation through an unusual catalytic cross‑dismutation of lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) and hydroperoxyl radicals (HOO•). Importantly, this potent chemical reactivity translates effectively into biological systems: Blatter radicals confer broad anti‑ferroptotic cytoprotection at low nanomolar concentrations, effectively protect against oxygen‑glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) injury, and exert strong anti‑inflammatory effects in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑stimulated BV2 microglial cells. Collectively, our results highlight the unprecedented versatility of Blatter radicals—extending from stable radicals to RTAs—and validate a rational design strategy for potent ferroptosis inhibitors.

item.title: Hydrogen‐Bond Encoding in a Structurally Minimal Cyclochiral Monomer Enables Assembly of Large Cavities Displaying Supramolecular Isomerism
item.description:
Minimalist design, maximal function: A structurally minimal flexible monomer encoding intra- and intermolecular hydrogen-bond motifs undergoes guest-driven self-sorting with fullerenes to form homochiral tetrameric capsules. Cyclochirality arises from restricted rotation, while cooperative H-bonding and C─H···π interactions stabilize inclusion complexes exhibiting a novel supramolecular isomerism. This work reveals that minimalistic monomer design can encode cavity-forming behavior.


ABSTRACT

Large, well-defined molecular cavities are typically constructed from rigid covalent scaffolds, which can limit structural adaptability and increase synthetic complexity. Here, we introduce a hydrogen-bond encoded supramolecular strategy that enables structurally minimal, flexible monomers to assemble into discrete fullerene-binding capsules. The monomer combines intra- and intermolecular hydrogen-bonding motifs that restrict conformational freedom, induce cyclochirality, and guide controlled self-assembly into oligomeric or cyclic aggregates. Spectroscopic and crystallographic analyses show that guest-induced self-sorting with fullerenes drives the formation of homochiral tetrameric capsules with high binding affinity and distinct structural isomerism. X-ray structures confirm compact host–guest complexes stabilized by cooperative hydrogen bonding and C─H···π interactions. This work demonstrates that minimal monomer design can encode complex supramolecular behaviour, providing an adaptive platform for molecular recognition, catalysis, and materials science.

item.title: Second‐Sphere Aromatic Substitutions That Tune H‐Atom Transfer Reactivity Observed for a Series of S = 1 Nonheme FeIV=O Complexes: An Enthalpy‐Entropy Compensation Effect
item.description:
A series of oxoiron(IV) complexes was synthesized to determine the impact of electronically tuned aromatic substitution in the secondary sphere of the ligand. Despite possessing identical electronic properties, they show significant differences in C─H oxidation reactions. A linear correlation between ΔH‡ and ΔS‡ was found, indicating enthalpy-entropy compensation in Hydrogen Atom Transfer reactivity, which is influenced by steric features.


ABSTRACT

Synthetic nonheme FeIV═O complexes reported thus far often have S = 1 ground states, demonstrating markedly lower oxidative reactivity in C─H bond breakage compared to their S = 2 counterparts. Recently, we have identified that incorporating cycloalkyl groups into the second coordination sphere of the nitrilotris(benzimidazole) ligand produce the most reactive FeIV═O complexes within the tripodal ligand family, exhibiting an S = 1 ground state. Here, we have synthesized six S = 1 complexes having the NTB ligand framework with either electron-rich or electron-poor aromatic groups in the secondary coordination sphere of the ligand. These complexes have been characterized by Mössbauer data at 4 K and 1H NMR spectra at 193 K with quite similar electronic characteristics despite having distinct electronically tuned ligands. Nevertheless, the complexes show substrate oxidation rates that differ by nearly an order of magnitude from each other, giving rise to a notable linear correlation between activation enthalpies and activation entropies of HAT reactions. These outcomes thus enable further investigation of the Enthalpy-Entropy Compensation Effect (EECE) in HAT reactions involving these oxoiron(IV) complexes. Finally, the role played by steric attributes of the secondary coordination sphere group in regulating the reactivity of this series of complexes has been explored.

item.title: Electronic Confinement Induced Single Atom Functionality in Hydroxylamine Synthesis Unveiled by Constant Potential Simulation
item.description:
Single-atom functionality does not require a predefined single-atom catalyst. Electronic confinement emerges through operando restructuring of transition metals, generating isolated metal centers that stabilize *HNO and promote hydroxylamine selectivity. This convergent catalytic behavior establishes electronic confinement as a general design strategy for generating single-atom functionality and engineering hydroxylamine-selective electrocatalysts beyond preformed SACs.


ABSTRACT

Electrochemical nitric oxide (NO) reduction offers a sustainable route for hydroxylamine (NH2OH) synthesis. Single-atom catalysts (SACs), featuring isolated metal centers and weaker adsorbate binding than extended metals, are widely regarded as ideal NH2OH-selective catalysts. However, the recent observation of NH2OH production on highly reactive metals challenges this conventional viewpoint and indicates that SACs are not indispensable in hydroxylamine electrosynthesis. Here, we establish a unified picture in which electronic confinement induces single-atom functionality that underlies NH2OH selectivity. Specifically, our constant-potential simulations identify the competition between *HNO and *NOH formation as a key determinant of NH2OH versus NH3 selectivity, with preferential *HNO formation directing the reaction toward NH2OH production. Grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations further reveal that highly reactive metals undergo operando surface restructuring, generating isolated metal centers that acquire single-atom functionality and preferentially stabilize *HNO. Electronic structure analysis uncovers a unified origin of *HNO preference: heteroatom coordination induces strong orbital hybridization, narrowing the metal d-band and localizing the electronic states of the isolated metal centers. This electronic confinement enables balanced *HNO-metal interactions while preserving the intramolecular N─O bond, thereby stabilizing *HNO and promoting NH2OH selectivity. These findings establish electronic confinement as a promising and general design principle for developing NH2OH-selective electrocatalysts beyond predefined SACs.

item.title: Superoxide‐Anion‐Dominated Labeling of Graphene Defects in an Interfacial Nanoreactor of Electron‐Donated Substrate
item.description:
A photochemical strategy is reported for the targeted labeling of graphene defects via spatially confined interfacial reactions. At defect sites, electron acquisition by photoexcited MB redirects the photosensitization pathway to Type I, generating •O2 − that locally etches the underlying copper, thereby transforming defects from passive structural features into chemically addressable sites for interfacial engineering of two-dimensional materials.


ABSTRACT

Harnessing the chemical reactivity of defects delivers a fundamental tool for precise nanoscale characterization of graphene defects. Herein, we develop a confined photochemical strategy based on the photosensitization of dye molecules targeted at the chemically active defects of graphene to label the defects. The graphene/copper interface enriches the electrons of graphene defects to construct a nanoreactor within defect-positioning interfaces, which modulates the preferential adsorption and the photosensitization reaction pathway of photoexcited methylene blue (MB). The nanoscale reactor preferentially channels the reaction through the Type I electron-transfer pathway, significantly triggering the •O2 − generation while concomitantly attenuating the competing Type II energy-transfer pathway. Subsequently, the •O2 − species deduce the selective etching reaction of Cu at defect sites, with the reaction kinetics following the Higuchi model. Moreover, the etching process exhibits pronounced crystallographic specificity, as evidenced by distinct pit morphologies and etching rates on the copper (111), (110), and (100) crystalline planes. DFT calculations confirm preferential adsorption and favorable electron transfer from defects to •O2 − species, unravelling the spatially confined nature of the etching reaction at graphene defects. Collectively, our results demonstrate how localized electronic states can dictate the interfacial reaction landscapes, advancing defect chemistry-guided identification/modification methodology of two-dimensional materials.

item.title: Inverse Solid‐State Photoluminescence and Electrochemiluminescence of Isostructural Nanoclusters: Unveiling the Critical Role of Intermolecular Charge Migration
item.description:
Strategic surface engineering modulation precisely tailors the supramolecular packing density of atomically precise AuAg nanoclusters, effectively breaking the conventional AIE-ECL trade-off. By comparing (AuAg)18 and (AuAg)17 systems, this study reveals that efficient charge transport facilitated by stronger π–π interactions far outweighs intrinsic luminescence efficiency in determining performance. Consequently, these findings provide novel and critical insights for the rational design and future development of high-performance solid-state electrochemiluminescent materials.


ABSTRACT

Atomically precise metal nanoclusters are promising electrochemiluminescent (ECL) materials. However, the correlation between their solid-state photoluminescence (PL) and ECL remains ambiguous, severely hindering the rational design of high-performance solid-state ECL materials. Herein, we report two nanoclusters, Au5Ag13(DPPP)4(C6F5S)10 and [AuxAg17-x ((DPPP)5(C6F5S)8]SbF6, which share an identical Au5Ag8 metal core but differ slightly in peripheral motifs, thus exhibiting a striking inverse solid-state PL–ECL relationship. Single-crystal structures and Hirshfeld surface analysis reveal that the stronger π–π interactions and higher molecular packing density in (AuAg)18 facilitate efficient intermolecular electron transfer and charge migration, which are more critical than excited-state generation and annihilation during the ECL process. This work demonstrates that charge transfer between nanoclusters and the electrode surface outweighs intrinsic excited-state annihilation and decay in solid-state ECL, providing a new mechanistic guideline for designing high-performance ECL materials beyond the traditional pursuit of strong PL.

item.title: Heavy‐Atom Tunneling at Room Temperature Revealed by Instanton Theory
item.description:
Usually, tunneling does not play a significant role in chemical reactions except at low temperature, especially when heavy atoms are involved. However, using nonadiabatic instanton theory we find that heavy-atom tunneling dominates the reaction mechanism for spin-forbidden processes in the synthesis of strained organic molecules even at room temperature.


ABSTRACT

Quantum-mechanical tunneling enables molecules to react even when their energy is below the activation barrier. Nonetheless, it is not normally expected that the dominant mechanism of chemical reactions relies on tunneling except at very low temperatures, especially when heavy atoms are involved. This assumption is valid for most adiabatic reactions proceeding on a single potential energy surface. However, we argue that heavy-atom tunneling at room temperature may be more important than previously supposed in the case of nonadiabatic processes, such as spin-forbidden reactions. In this work, we employ a recently developed computational approach (called nonadiabatic instanton theory) to capture the optimal multidimensional tunneling pathway for the ring closing of various strained organic triplet diradicals to form housane and a cage dione (which is a precursor for cubane). Surprisingly, we find that these reactions are dominated by the tunneling of heavy carbon atoms even at room temperature.
